[p. 327] **Sūrat Tabbat**

Its purpose is the decisive, categorical certainty of the loss of the disbeliever, even if he were the closest of creation to the greatest of the successful. What follows from this is that the Lawgiver of the religion possesses a greatness that description falls short of. He does what He wills, because He has no equal whatsoever. This is an exhortation to monotheism (tawhid) among all the servants. For this reason, Sūrat al-Ikhlās is placed between the two surahs that affirm the guarantee of victory and the abundance of helpers. Its name, Tabbat, clearly indicates this when one reflects on the surah in this form: "In the name of God," the Compeller, the Proud, the Misleader, the Guide, "the Most Merciful," who extended to friend and foe alike the blessing of eloquent speech after the honour of existence, "the Most Compassionate," who singled out for success those who love Him.

* *

When the Glorified and Exalted, in Sūrat al-Naṣr, had announced with certainty the achievement of victory for the people of this religion after the humiliation they had endured, and had given the decisive command to increase their numbers after the paucity that had afflicted them along with humiliation, and concluded it by saying that He is the Oft-Returning (al-Tawwāb), Abū Lahab, owing to his extreme obstinacy toward this religion and his harm to the Imam of the Prophet (ﷺ), the lord of all worlds, despite being close to him, occupied a position that cannot be unknown, rather it was widely spread and famous, and he burned hearts and melted them. He was in a state such that people asked about his condition at that time: would he remain steadfast upon it, or would he be humiliated? So this surah relieved the rancour of this question, and it removed it through what would be for him of punishment. This was so that, after the occurrence of the conquest, the descent of triumph and victory, and the prevalence over enemies with might and subjugation, it would remind the Prophet (ﷺ) of what had been at the outset of the matter of their tyranny, their harm, and their strength in numbers and equipment, and that none of that availed them anything. Rather, God fulfilled His promise in His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered to Hell, and wretched is the resting-place﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 12]. And they were lying in what they were engaged in of mutual support, assistance, alliance, and pact. Thus He mentioned his enemies toward him and those nearest to him by lineage, as an indication that there is no difference in their denial of him between the near and the distant, and that his closeness to him did not benefit him, so that this would move the people of the religion to strive in action without relying upon any means or lineage other than what He, Glorified is He, had legislated. He, Exalted, spoke in the past tense, indicating that the matter has already been decreed and completed, so there is no escape and no avoiding it: ﴿Tabbat﴾, that is, the greatest severing and the most complete decisive ending have occurred, for it has failed and lost the utmost loss. This is what leads to ruin, because there is no salvation except the salvation of the Hereafter. He made the address of this surah come from God and did not open it with "Say" as its sisters do, because this is more courteous, more fitting in the category of excuse, and more appropriate in observing the ties of kinship. For this reason He did not repeat its mention in the Qur'an. It is also more emphatic in God's, Glorified and Exalted, support of him (ﷺ), and closer to warning and to permitting the swiftness of its occurrence.

Since the hand is the locus of human power, when it is disabled his affairs are disabled, so how much more so when the disablement occurs in both hands together. He said, indicating by the dual form the generality of his ruin, that his strength did not avail him anything, and because the dual is used to express the self (nafs). He also indicated by the kunya, though it is usually used for honour, the correspondence of his name to his condition and its harmony, which necessitates his great punishment: ﴿The two hands of Abū Lahab﴾. So he has no power to give or to withhold, nor to bring benefit or avert harm. It is also an indication that the beauty of his appearance did not avail him anything of the ugliness of his conduct, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed God does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

Because he was called by this kunya for the brightness of his face and the glowing of his cheeks, and because it is more widely known, so explanation by it is stronger and clearer. And the expression by it, though it is clearer, is more fitting in the saying of "that which is best" (al-latī hiya aḥsan). For his name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, which is ugly and necessitates turning away from it out of jealousy for servanthood, lest it be attributed to other than its rightful possessor.

[p. 330] Imam Abū Jaʿfar Ibn al-Zubayr said: "This surah, although it was revealed for a particular cause and in a known story, is, together with what precedes it and is connected to it, as if it were said: 'Your lifespan has ended, O Muhammad, and what you were entrusted with of the great trust of the Message has come to its end; He commanded you, you have conveyed what you bore, and your term has arrived. The sign of this is people entering the religion of God in multitudes and their responding after their hesitation. Woe to whoever opposes you and turns away from following you, even if he is the closest of people to you.' Surah ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 1] has separated between your friends and your enemies, and by it the ruling on whoever follows you from among those who opposed you became clear. For this reason, upon him be prayer and peace, it was called the one that frees from hypocrisy. So that the disbelievers of Quraysh and others would know that no one is protected from the Fire except by faith, and that kinship is neither beneficial nor effective in anything except with faith: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 6]; ﴿You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do﴾ [Yūnus: 41]; ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71]. Here the Book ends in its entirety." End of quotation.

Since it might be thought that tabāb is specific to destruction, and that it refers to the literal destruction of the two hands, and since a person does not lose all benefit by losing his two hands, though these may be used to express the self, He said, stating the intended meaning explicitly: ﴿And he perished﴾, that is, he himself, in his entirety, is in complete ruin and loss. By this He realised what was intended by the ascription to the two hands, namely the metaphor for a ruin after which there is no survival. Evidently the first (tabbat) is a supplication and the second (tabb) is a report. And from this one knows that affiliation to the righteous does not benefit unless one follows them in their deeds, for he was the paternal uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The root ṯ-b-b and b-t-t, which combines the letters tāʾ and bāʾ for the two causes, the lower inward and the higher outward, revolves around severance which in most of its states leads to destruction, for whoever cuts himself off toward the means while turning away from their Causer is in the greatest tabāb (ruin). Sometimes severance is by gathering all the means, so that need arises concerning aims and beloved things. Ibn Makkūm said in al-Jamʿ bayn al-Muḥkam wa-l-ʿUbāb: "Tabb and tabāb: loss. Tabban lahu, as a supplication; tabban tabīban, as an intensive." Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Qazzāz said: "It is as if you said: 'loss for him,' and it is the verbal noun, placed in the accusative like saqyan lahu." Ibn Durayd said: "It seems that tabb is the verbal noun and tibāb is the noun; and tabab, tibāb, and tabīb: destruction, and tatbīb: deficiency and loss." All of this is clear in severance from good and success. He said: "And al-tābb is the old man among men, and the female is tābbah." Al-Qazzāz said: "When you ask a man about a woman, you say: 'Is she ushābbah or tābbah?', that is, is she an aged, decrepit old woman?" It is known that advanced age is close to severance and destruction. Al-tābb is also the weak, and the plural is atbāb (Hudhalī usage). A donkey whose back is worn (tābb al-ẓahr) when its rear is galled; and a camel tābb in this manner is a rare usage. There is no doubt that galling and weakness are destruction in meaning.

Tabba: severed, like batta. That is, with the preceding bāʾ; and they fell into a disastrous tabūb, and he is in tabbah, that is, in a severe condition. Al-tabbiyy, with fatḥa or kasra, is a kind of date of Bahrain, said to be inferior, eaten by the scraps of people. Atabba Allāh quwwatahu: He weakened his strength. Tabbabūhum tatbīban: they destroyed them. Tabbaba: he aged. All of this is clear in severance to ruin and loss. Al-tabawwub, with ḍamma, means what the ribs enfold, like the chest and the heart. This admits of good and evil, for when the heart is corrupted the whole body is corrupted, and when it is sound the whole body is sound. Then the severance would be to success and salvation; or because the folding of the ribs over it is a separation from the outside. Istatabba al-amr: it became prepared and level. Al-Qazzāz said: "It is said: this cause does not hold (lā tastatibb) in analogues of this statement," that is, it does not operate in its analogues. It is as if it is of the category of removal, since the sīn, when it joins the letter of the two causes, announces success and victory and salvation, for it is a letter that indicates completeness in informing about a thing, in completion and in familiarity. Better than this is that when it operates in analogues it clarifies them and uncovers their meanings, separating them and making them clear, and cutting them off from non-analogues by removing the confusion they had with them.

What confirms the meanings of tabb and clarifies that it returns to severance is its reversal, which is batt, with the bāʾ placed first, which is the outward cause that is stronger, insofar as it is not realised except with the complete inward cause. It is said: batta al-shayʾ yabutthu battan, and abattahu: he severed it with a complete uprooting severance; batta huwa yabutt, and bayyatta battan, and infatta. Perhaps the intransitive and the augmented forms are equal in transitivity, indicating that what is achieved by the bare form of severance is of such perfection that nothing more can be added to it. Likewise, the intransitive form in its bare and reflexive forms is equal to the transitive form in the basic meaning. And ṣadaqahu battah: a complete divorce, separating him from its companion. He divorced her three times with a final divorce (battatan wa-ibtātan), that is, a severance with no return in it. And "I will not do it at all (al-battah)" as if he cut off his action. Sībawayh said: "They said qaʿada al-battah," a verbal noun for emphasis, used only with the definite article. Batta ʿalayhi al-qaḍāʾ battan and abattahu: he severed it. Sakrān mā yabutt kalāman: a drunk who does not sever his speech, and what is not severed (yubatt) by him. Al-Qazzāz said: "yabutt is from abatta, and yabutt is from batta." Sakrān bātt: one cut off from acting because of drunkenness. Abatta yamīnahu: he executed it, that is, severed it from breaking. Batt-at hiya: she became obligated and was made lawful with a final severance, and all of this is from severance. Abatta biʿīrahu: he severed it by travelling. Al-munbatt in the hadith: the one who wearied his mount until its back was ruined and he was left cut off with it. Al-Qazzāz said: "He is the one who wearied his mount until he severed its back, and so he remained munbatt with it, that is, cut off with it." Batta ʿalayhi al-shahādah and abattahā: he severed upon him with it and obliged him to it. Batta ʿalayhi al-qaḍāʾ and abattahu: he severed it. Al-bātt: the emaciated one who cannot stand, as if his strength has been cut off. And in the hadith: "There is no fast for one who has not severed (yabutt) the fast from the night," meaning: it makes it obligatory, that is, he cuts it upon himself before dawn, from abatta ʿalayhi al-ḥukm when he severed it. It is also narrated as yabutt, from batta when he severed; both have the same meaning, and they are two eloquent dialects. It is narrated in the hadith "man lam yabutt" from al-bayāt (overnight intention). And aḥmaq bātt: extremely foolish, so said al-Layth; al-Azharī said it is tābb with the bāʾ postponed. Al-batt: a thick, coarse, square, green cloak; it is said to be of wool and fleece, and its plural is butūt. Al-battāt, with lightening: the household goods and provisions, as if it cuts its owner off from need. Battatūhu: they provided him, or that this is from removal, because it is a connection to its owner and a support. Induction establishes that every root has a predominant meaning around which it revolves, and within it is something for the removal of that meaning. Fulān ʿalā battāt amr: when he is about to finish it, for then he is cut off. You say: "I ground with the millstone battan," when you begin turning it from your left, as if it indicates severance by the completion of resolve, since this is stronger and more feasible for the grinder. Inbatta al-rajul: the water of his back was cut off. It is said: "This is a battan rope," when it is a single strand, as if, since it is thus and easily severed, severance is attributed to it in hyperbole, like ʿadl. And Fulān inbatta ʿan Fulān: when he is cut off and withdraws."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 111, verse 2:

When Allah (glorified is He) stated his destruction in this emphatic form, given that the owner of the story and others among the disbelievers denied the message through the language of their condition and through their claim, because of his wealth and children and the strength he had in numbers and equipment, this increased the matter's certainty, informing that worldly conditions offer no sufficiency. So He said, informing or asking in denial, ﴿What his wealth availed him﴾, meaning, what sufficed and substituted and took the place of, ﴿against him﴾, meaning against Abu Lahab the wretched, the expelled, the one distanced from mercy and destined for punishment, ﴿his wealth﴾, meaning the abundant wealth which custom holds will save one from destruction.

Since acquisition (kasb) is more general than wealth, and wealth may acquire benefits greater than itself, such as status and other things, and since a person may be successful without wealth through matters achieved by his own effort that lie outside wealth, He said, explaining this and clarifying that only what Allah has commanded benefits, ﴿nor what he earned﴾, meaning even if that was in a tremendous form of children, companions and honour among his clan, whom he pleased by following (p-٣٣٦) the Prophet (ﷺ) in gatherings, while he harmed and denied him and forbade people from believing him, although previously he had called him "the truthful, the trustworthy." His son Utba was severely harmful to the Prophet (ﷺ), until the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Abu Lahab knew that this supplication would surely reach him. When the matter drew near, and the time came for what the one of lofty honour intended, he arranged for him to travel to Syria. His father entrusted him to the travelling companions so that they might save him despite this supplication. They would surround him when he slept so that he would be in their midst, the loads encircling him while they encircled the loads, and the riding beasts encircling them. But that did not benefit him. Rather, a lion came, sniffed the people until it reached him, and tore off his head. That did not benefit his father either, rather he persisted in his misguidance because of what had preceded in Allah's knowledge, until the battle of Badr occurred, and he did not go out to it. When the fugitives came back, among them was his nephew Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith. He said, "Come here, nephew, for you have the news." He said, "Yes! By Allah, it was only that when we met them, we gave them our backs, they took us as they wished, [and they took us captive as they wished -]. Yet, by Allah, I was weary of people. We met men, white, on piebald horses, between the sky and the earth, nothing could stand before them and nothing remained [i.e. -] what they left behind (p-٣٣٧) and nothing could stand against them." Abu Rafi', the slave of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (may Allah be pleased with him), who was sitting in a room in the mosque sharpening arrows, said: Islam had already entered our household, and we were concealing our Islam. I could not restrain myself and said, "By Allah, those were the angels." He said: Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. He said: I grappled with him, and he lifted me and threw me to the ground, then sat upon me striking me, and I was a weak man. Then Umm al-Fadl, meaning his mistress, the wife of al-Abbas (may Allah be pleased with her), rose to a pillar of the room, meaning the tent, and struck him with it a blow that split his head with a grievous wound, and said, "You thought him weak, enemy of Allah, now that his master is absent." So he rose, fleeing in humiliation. By Allah, he did not live more than seven or six nights, until Allah struck him with the 'adasah and killed him, and his distancing himself from danger by staying behind from Badr did not benefit him. The 'adasah is a pustule resembling a lentil that emerges in places on the body, of the same kind as plague, and it usually kills. Al-Qazzaz said: It used to be contagious in the Jahiliyyah, and hardly anyone escaped it. One says: "'adasa al-rajul," so he is "ma'dus," just as one says "ta'ana" so he is "matun," when the plague strikes him. End of quotation.

Because of the Arabs' pessimism about it, Abu Lahab was left unburied for three days (p-٣٣٨) until he became putrid. Then they hired some of the Sudanese until they buried him. It is said that they dug a pit far from him because of the intensity of his stench, then pushed him with long poles until they threw him into it, and pelted him with stones and dirt from a distance until they covered him. That became a practice in stoning him, so he is stoned until now. This is among the first signs of the miraculousness of these verses: that he became a disgrace among the Arabs, [without -] anything availing him [of what he supposed would avail him -].

﴿He will burn in a Fire﴾ — and when Allah, glorified and exalted, informed of the occurrence of this greatest destruction for him, and since no punishment is comparable to the punishment of the Hereafter, He explained it with His words: ﴿He will burn in a Fire﴾, i.e., soon, by a promise that admits no failure. ﴿A Fire﴾, i.e., he will be thrust into it, and it will envelop him and surround him.

Since the aim is the intensity of his torment with the most intense heat, just as it burned the hearts of the friends (of Allah), and since a fire may be an ember that goes out soon, He said: ﴿of blazing flame﴾, i.e., it will never subside or die down, because that is what the companionship expressed by "dhat" (possessor of) implies. This is after his death. There is no definitive proof in the surah that he will not believe, since it is possible that the one who burns does so for wickedness. So there is no proof in it for one who says that it contains a charge to do what is known to be impossible, so that he would be commanded to believe while it is known that he is judged not to believe (p-339). Although Allah verified this report by his death as a disbeliever in the second year of the Hijrah (the migration), after the Battle of Badr, which was the fifteenth year of prophethood, his disbelief was known to be decisively fixed only by his dying as a disbeliever, not by anything in this surah or elsewhere.

Among the wonders: the words related to him in this surah are fifteen words, so they indicate the year of his death, after he had seen his destruction with his own eyes at Badr and elsewhere. When we add to them the four words of the basmala (the formula "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"), it corresponds to the sixth year of the Hijrah, the year of the 'Umrah of Hudaybiyyah, the year of the causal conquest (al-Fath al-Sababi), in which his destruction [and loss] was realized for everyone who has faith in the unseen and repels doubt. When you add to them the two explicit pronouns, which are closer to the terminological words than the concealed ones, it corresponds to the eighth year of the Hijrah, in which the true conquest (of Makkah) took place, so that everything revealed about him in this surah came true among the Quraysh entirely.

When you add the three concealed pronouns, it corresponds to the eleventh year, on the basis that if you begin with the concealed pronouns, the correspondence also results. That is, it corresponds to the ninth year, the year of the delegations, in which people entered the religion in multitudes, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) performed the Hajj with the people as commander, and at the season it was proclaimed (the declaration of Bara'ah, "Disavowal"), and that no polytheist should perform Hajj after that year. Thus the failure of Abu Lahab was realized for everyone who attended the season, especially whoever knew of his circling behind the Prophet (ﷺ) and his denial of him, among Muslims and others. When we add to that the two explicit pronouns, it corresponds to the eleventh year, the first year of the caliphate of al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), in which the entire Arabian Peninsula was brought under control after Satan had toyed with many of its people.

So they returned after Allah had killed those among them whom He knew to be created for Hell. Then the destruction of Abu Lahab, and the fire of blazing flame, were realized for all the Arabs, through their general acceptance of faith in the eleventh year of the Hijrah, after twenty-three years had passed since the prophethood. The matter was then settled, and it was known that the religion had firmly established its tent-pegs and its pillar was secure, and that He who protected it during the life of the Prophet (ﷺ) protected it after him. He, glorified, is Living and does not die, and is Capable, nothing overcomes Him.

The number of words in the surah is twenty-three, which corresponds to the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, the tenth year, which is the twenty-third year from the mission (al-ba'thah), in which the religion was perfected, the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that Satan had despaired of being worshipped in the land of the Arabs. Thus the destruction of Abu Lahab was realized for all people, especially whoever attended the season, the man who used to circle behind the Prophet (ﷺ) in those gatherings, denying him and harming him.

Indeed in that is a lesson.

Since al-Biqa'i had reported Allah's words about him, the perfection of ruin, which is the extreme of loss, and since the hardest thing for a person is the violation of what protects his womenfolk, to the point that he would give his own life rather than allow it, especially among the Arabs, for none come close to them in this, He increased his contempt by mentioning the one who protects her. He described her with the worst and most reprehensible image. He said, indicating that keeping company with evildoers is the utmost loss, for even a good disposition may be corrupted by a bad one, so how much more when the companion is bad? And indeed, pleasing people by means that anger Allah is the greatest destruction. ﴿And his wife﴾, that is, Umm Jamil, the sister of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb ibn Umayya ibn Abd Shams ibn Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy, shared her husband's ruin and burning, and nothing of her wealth, lineage or nobility could avail her. He turned away from mentioning her by her kunya (teknonym, a respectful name formed from a parent's title), because her attribute was ugliness, which is the opposite of her kunya. From this is derived the disapproval of giving someone a title such as "Helper of the Religion" or the like when he does not possess the quality its title indicates. Then he described her with what her sin pointed to and completed the ugliness of her image, saying: ﴿the carrier of firewood﴾, that is, the one who carries the most that can be carried of the firewood of Hell, by what she used to walk with and exaggerate in, namely carrying the firewood of slander and tale-bearing, with which she stirred up enmity against the Prophet (ﷺ), the severity of his harm, and the kindling of the fire of war and hostility against him (ﷺ). From the saying of the poet:

"From the white ones, who did not hunt upon the back of his mother,
nor walk among the tribe with fresh firewood."

He meant tale-bearing. He expressed it with "fresh" to indicate the increase of evil in it through its smoke. Slander was likened to firewood because it kindles evil and separates people, just as firewood becomes fuel for fire and so disperses it. Likewise, she used to carry thorns and scatter them at night on the path of the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to harm him. She did this herself out of the intensity of her enmity and carried it out at night so as to conceal it, because she was of noble standing. When the surah was revealed, it depicted her in the most ugly image, and [that] was the greatest exposure of her. The reading of ʿĀṣim with the accusative (naṣb) by way of qaṭʿ (grammatical disjunction, detaching the word from the preceding case) on censure implies that ﴿his wife﴾ is a subject (مُبْتَدَأٌ) and that the predicate (الخَبَرَ)

﴿in her neck﴾, i.e., her neck, and its finest part. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) on the first interpretation. ﴿a rope﴾ like that of woodcutters, to belittle her affair and demean her state. ﴿of palm fiber﴾, i.e., fiber, or the fiber of the muqill (the doum palm), or of something that has been twisted and whose twisting has been made firm, from their saying: "a man of masdūd character," i.e., firmly twisted and well-knit. The last part of the surah has returned to its first part, for whoever has a wife depicted as a woman of firewood, carrying a bundle of wood on her back with a rope hung around her neck, is in the utmost degradation, ruin, baseness and loss.

The overall theme of this surah is that Abū Lahab cut off his kinship ties, deviated from the right path, and, after his own misguidance, strove to misguide others. He also wronged the sincere advisor who was kind to him and who spared no effort in counseling him, as you see, while he himself spared no effort in harming him. He relied on his wealth and gains, so he perished and brought his wife down with him, along with whoever followed him among his children. Among the greatest aims of Surah al-Nisā' (which corresponds to it, answering its conclusion to its opening) are kinship, closeness, and kindness, especially toward relatives, and justice in all words and deeds. Thus the description of the state of the sincere advisor, who does not speak from desire, and the state of the misguided one, who speaks only from desire, is found in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you and to guide you to the ways of those before you﴾ [al-Nisā': 26]. Its conclusion is a warning against imitating his condition, as though it were said: Allah makes clear to you that if you go astray you will be like Abū Lahab in ruin, and burning in the Fire, as has become clear to you. So be on guard against everything that resembles his condition, even if it appears to you otherwise, for I know better than you, and Allah is All-Knowing of everything. "And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

(p. 343)
